goals: Define the Reformation and state when it began
Explain the practices of the Church that critics objected to
Explain the role of the new learning, earlier reformers, rulers and merchants

slides.heading: The Reformation: meaning and causes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what the Reformation was and why it began.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the meaning and date of the Reformation, the Church practices critics objected to, the new learning, and other causes
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we learn what the Reformation was and why it began in fifteen seventeen. We study the practices of the Church that critics objected to, the new learning, and other causes such as rulers, merchants and earlier reformers. For every tradition we use respectful and neutral words.

slides.heading: What was the Reformation?
slides.body_md: Learn this definition well; it is a favourite exam point.

rows: Protested against certain practices of the Roman Catholic Church

visual.alt: Table on the Reformation: a sixteenth-century movement in Western Christianity that protested against certain practices of the Roman Catholic Church, led to Protestant churches, and began in 1517

slides.narration: The Reformation was a movement of the sixteenth century in Western Christianity. It protested against certain practices of the Roman Catholic Church and led to the formation of Protestant churches. It began in the year fifteen seventeen. Notice the careful word certain: the protest was about particular practices.

visual.alt: Causes web: the Reformation at the centre, with four boxes around it: Church practices objected to, the new learning, earlier reformers, and rulers and merchants
visual.caption: Causes of the Reformation at a glance.

slides.narration: Look at the web. Four groups of causes worked together. There were practices of the Church that critics objected to. There was the new learning. There were earlier reformers. And there were rulers and merchants with their own interests. No single cause explains everything.

slides.heading: Practices critics objected to: indulgences and offices
bullets: **Indulgences**: certificates said to reduce punishment for sins.
**Simony**: the sale of Church offices.
Critics objected that these seemed to put a price on forgiveness and posts.

rows: Certificates said to reduce punishment for sins
Forgiveness seemed to be sold for money
Posts went to those who paid, not those best suited

visual.alt: Table of two practices critics objected to: the sale of indulgences, certificates said to reduce punishment for sins, and simony, the sale of Church offices, with what critics said about each

slides.narration: First, indulgences. These were certificates said to reduce punishment for sins, and critics objected to their sale for money. Second, simony, which means the sale of Church offices. Critics said posts could go to those who paid rather than to those best suited. Always say critics objected, which keeps your wording neutral.

slides.heading: Practices critics objected to: wealth, lives, courts, Latin
bullets: The **great wealth and taxes** of the Church, such as the **tithe**.
The **worldly lives** of some clergy.
**Church courts**.
Services and the Bible in **Latin**.

rows: The great wealth of the Church and taxes such as the tithe
Some clergy lived in ways critics thought unsuited to their calling
Their authority over many matters of daily life
Services and the Bible in Latin, which ordinary people did not understand

visual.alt: Table of four further practices: the wealth and taxes of the Church, the worldly lives of some clergy, the authority of Church courts, and services and the Bible in Latin

slides.narration: Critics also pointed to the great wealth and taxes of the Church, such as the tithe, which was about one tenth of produce or income. They noted the worldly lives of some clergy, and the authority of Church courts. And they observed that services and the Bible were in Latin, which ordinary people did not understand.

slides.heading: Quick check: a certificate
slides.body_md: Name the practice, and say why critics objected.
slides.narration: Read about the baker and his certificate. Name the practice, and then think about what critics objected to in its sale.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from scene to practice
slides.body_md: Read the scene, find the practice, then state it neutrally.
bullets: Step 1 — What exactly is happening?
Step 2 — Is it money, a post, a tax or a language?
Step 3 — Name the practice.
Step 4 — Write: critics objected to this.

rows: A farmer in Linden hands over a tenth of his grain
A post in Lindenmark goes to whoever pays most
A villager in Linden holds a certificate bought from a seller
A shepherd cannot follow the Latin in his village church

visual.alt: Table sorting four imagined scenes: a tenth of grain is the tithe, a post to the highest payer is simony, a bought certificate is an indulgence, and Latin not understood is the language criticism

slides.narration: Use four steps. First, see what exactly is happening. Second, decide whether it is about money, a post, a tax or a language. Third, name the practice. Fourth, write that critics objected to it. A tenth of grain is the tithe. A post for the highest payer is simony. A bought certificate is an indulgence.

slides.heading: The new learning: the spirit of enquiry
slides.body_md: The **Renaissance** is only background here: its spirit of enquiry encouraged people to **question authority**.

visual.alt: Flow: the Renaissance spirit of enquiry led people to question authority, so Church practices were examined
visual.caption: The spirit of enquiry.

slides.narration: The Renaissance was a movement of new learning. Here we need only its spirit of enquiry. People were encouraged to ask questions and to question authority, and so they also began to examine Church practices. The Renaissance has its own chapter. For now, treat it as background.

slides.heading: Erasmus and the humanists
bullets: **Humanist** scholars studied old writings with care.
**Erasmus** was a **Dutch** scholar.
His work **The Praise of Folly** (about **1511**) criticised abuses.

rows: His writings criticised abuses and encouraged people to question

visual.alt: Table on Erasmus: a Dutch humanist scholar, author of The Praise of Folly about 1511, whose writings criticised abuses and encouraged people to question

slides.narration: Humanist scholars studied old writings with great care. One famous humanist was Erasmus, a Dutch scholar. His book The Praise of Folly, written about fifteen eleven, criticised abuses. Remember that Erasmus did not found a Protestant church; he contributed by encouraging people to question.

slides.heading: Printing
slides.body_md: **Printing** spread critical ideas and Bibles **quickly**.

nodes.label: The printing press makes many copies

visual.alt: Flow: scribes copy by hand slowly, the printing press makes many copies, and pamphlets and Bibles spread quickly
visual.caption: Printing.

slides.narration: Before printing, books were copied by hand, which was slow. A printing press could make many copies in a short time. Pamphlets and Bibles could therefore reach many more readers, and critical ideas spread quickly across towns and countries.

slides.heading: Quick check: printing
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true.
slides.narration: Check each statement on its own first. Then ask whether the reason explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Earlier reformers
slides.body_md: Dissatisfaction was not new. Remember the two names and their countries.

rows: An English translation of the Bible

visual.alt: Table of two earlier reformers: John Wycliffe in England in the fourteenth century, with an English translation of the Bible, and Jan Hus in Bohemia in the early fifteenth century

slides.narration: Unease with certain practices was older than Luther. John Wycliffe in England, in the fourteenth century, is remembered for an English translation of the Bible. Jan Hus in Bohemia, in the early fifteenth century, also questioned some Church practices. For your exam, the names, countries and times are enough.

slides.heading: Rulers and merchants
bullets: **Rulers** of growing nation-states wanted control over **Church lands** and **appointments**.
**Merchants** resented Church **taxes**.

nodes.label: Rulers want control of Church lands and appointments

visual.alt: Flow: nation-states grow stronger, rulers want control of Church lands and appointments, and merchants resent Church taxes
visual.caption: Rulers and merchants.

slides.narration: Not every cause was about belief. Rulers of growing nation states wanted control over Church lands and over appointments in their kingdoms. Merchants resented the taxes they paid to the Church, which reduced their profits. These interests joined the religious causes.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sort the causes
slides.body_md: Place each cause in its group.
bullets: Step 1 — Is it about Church practice, learning, history or interests?
Step 2 — Put it in the group.
Step 3 — Check you have all four groups.

rows: Indulgences, simony, wealth and taxes, worldly lives, courts, Latin
Renaissance spirit of enquiry, Erasmus, printing
Wycliffe in England, Hus in Bohemia

visual.alt: Table grouping the causes: Church practices, the new learning, earlier reformers, and political and economic causes, each with examples

slides.narration: To revise, sort the causes into four groups. Church practices include indulgences, simony, wealth and taxes, worldly lives, courts and Latin. The new learning includes the spirit of enquiry, Erasmus and printing. Earlier reformers are Wycliffe and Hus. And political and economic causes are rulers and merchants.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the result
slides.body_md: Find the item that is a later result, not a cause.
slides.narration: Think about dates. A cause comes before the Reformation or at its start. Which item came after?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: planning a 10-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: (i) Three practices objected to. [3] (ii) The new learning. [3] (iii) Rulers, merchants, earlier reformers. [4]
bullets: (i) Indulgences, simony, wealth and taxes.
(ii) Enquiry, Erasmus, printing.
(iii) Rulers; merchants; Wycliffe and Hus.
One clear point for each mark.

visual.alt: Table planning a ten-mark answer: part (i) three practices for 3 marks, part (ii) the new learning for 3 marks, part (iii) rulers, merchants and earlier reformers for 4 marks

slides.narration: Plan a ten mark answer in three parts. Part one gives three practices that critics objected to. Part two explains the new learning with the spirit of enquiry, Erasmus and printing. Part three covers rulers, merchants and the earlier reformers Wycliffe and Hus. Give one clear point for each mark.

slides.heading: Quick check: match scene and cause
slides.body_md: Match each scene with its cause.
slides.narration: Use the groups of causes you have just learned. Match each scene with the cause it shows.

slides.heading: Writing about the causes neutrally
slides.body_md: Neutral wording earns marks and shows respect.

rows: Critics objected to certain practices, such as the sale of indulgences
Reformers protested against certain practices and proposed changes
Protestant churches formed from the movement

visual.alt: Table of neutral wording: instead of saying the Church was corrupt, write that critics objected to certain practices; instead of calling reformers rebels, write that they protested and proposed changes; instead of saying Protestants were right, write that Protestant churches formed

slides.narration: In a history answer, avoid sweeping words. Instead of saying the Church was corrupt, write that critics objected to certain practices. Instead of calling reformers rebels, write that they protested and proposed changes. Instead of saying one side was right, write that Protestant churches formed. This is both accurate and respectful.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: **Reformation**: a 16th-century movement; began in **1517**; led to **Protestant** churches.
Practices critics objected to: **indulgences**, **simony**, **wealth and taxes**, **worldly lives**, **courts**, **Latin**.
New learning: **enquiry**, **Erasmus**, **printing**.
Also: **Wycliffe** and **Hus**, **rulers**, **merchants**.

rows: Indulgences, simony, wealth and taxes, worldly lives, courts, Latin
Renaissance spirit of enquiry, Erasmus, printing
Wycliffe in England, Hus in Bohemia

visual.alt: Table grouping the causes: Church practices, the new learning, earlier reformers, and political and economic causes, each with examples

slides.narration: To sum up. The Reformation was a sixteenth century movement that began in fifteen seventeen and led to Protestant churches. Critics objected to practices such as indulgences, simony, wealth and taxes, worldly lives, courts and Latin. The new learning, earlier reformers, rulers and merchants also played a part.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Say **about** with approximate dates; give **1517** for the beginning.
Write **critics objected to**, never sweeping words.
Group causes into **practices, learning, earlier reformers, interests**.
Name **Erasmus** with **The Praise of Folly**; name **Wycliffe** and **Hus** with countries.
Mention the Renaissance only as **background**.
slides.narration: Some exam habits. Add the word about to approximate dates, and give fifteen seventeen for the beginning. Write that critics objected, never use sweeping words. Group the causes. Name Erasmus with his book, and Wycliffe and Hus with their countries. Mention the Renaissance only as background.

slides.heading: Martin Luther
bullets: A German **monk** and **professor** at **Wittenberg**.

rows: A monk and a professor at Wittenberg

visual.alt: Table of facts on Martin Luther: 1483 to 1546, German, a monk and professor at Wittenberg, known for the Ninety-five Theses of 1517

slides.narration: Martin Luther lived from fourteen eighty three to fifteen forty six. He was a German monk and a professor at the university of Wittenberg. In history, he is remembered for the protest he made public in fifteen seventeen, and for the teachings that followed from it.

slides.heading: 1517: the Ninety-five Theses
slides.body_md: Johann Tetzel was selling indulgences in Germany. Luther made public his **Ninety-five Theses** against their sale.

nodes.label: Johann Tetzel sells indulgences in Germany
Luther makes the Ninety-five Theses public, 1517
Protest against the sale of indulgences

visual.alt: Flow: Johann Tetzel sells indulgences in Germany, Luther makes the Ninety-five Theses public in 1517, the protest is against the sale of indulgences, and printing spreads the ideas
visual.caption: The protest of 1517.

slides.narration: In fifteen seventeen, Johann Tetzel was selling indulgences in Germany. Luther made public the Ninety five Theses, which were statements for debate against the sale of indulgences. Printing carried his ideas quickly to many readers. Remember: the Theses protested against the sale, and you do not need to learn their text.

slides.heading: 1521 and after
bullets: **Pope Leo X** excommunicated Luther (**1521**).
At the **Diet of Worms** (**1521**) he refused to take back his views.
**Frederick of Saxony** protected him.
He translated the **New Testament** into German, and later the whole Bible.

nodes.label: Diet of Worms, 1521: refuses to take back his views
Translates the New Testament into German

visual.alt: Flow: excommunicated by Pope Leo X in 1521, refuses to take back his views at the Diet of Worms in 1521, is protected by Frederick of Saxony, and translates the New Testament into German
visual.caption: From 1521 onwards.

slides.narration: In fifteen twenty one, Pope Leo the Tenth excommunicated Luther. At the Diet of Worms, an assembly of German princes and officials, Luther refused to take back his views. Frederick of Saxony protected him. During this time he translated the New Testament into German, and later the whole Bible.

slides.heading: Quick check: the assembly of 1521
slides.body_md: Name the assembly and the monk.
slides.narration: Read the clerk's diary. Think about the year, the place and who refused to take back his writings.

slides.heading: Luther's main teachings
slides.body_md: Five teachings: **faith**, the **Bible**, **priesthood of all believers**, **fewer sacraments**, **local language**.

notes.title: The Modern Age in Europe: Reformation — notes

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and practices critics objected to
sections.body_md:
- **Reformation:** a **16th-century movement** in Western Christianity that **protested against certain practices of the Roman Catholic Church** and led to the formation of **Protestant churches**. It began in **1517**.
- Practices critics objected to: the **sale of indulgences**; the **sale of Church offices** (simony); the **great wealth and taxes** of the Church (for example the tithe); the **worldly lives** of some clergy; **Church courts**; **services and the Bible in Latin**, which ordinary people did not understand.
- Use neutral wording: write that **critics objected to** these practices.

key_terms.definition_md: A 16th-century movement in Western Christianity that began in 1517.
A certificate said to reduce punishment for sins.
A Church tax of about one tenth of produce or income.

rows: Protested against certain practices of the Roman Catholic Church

sections.heading: 2. The new learning and other causes
sections.body_md:
- **New learning:** the Renaissance spirit of enquiry encouraged people to question authority (the Renaissance is background only). **Erasmus**, a Dutch humanist, criticised abuses in **The Praise of Folly** (about 1511). **Printing** spread critical ideas and Bibles quickly.
- **Earlier reformers:** **John Wycliffe** in England (14th century; an English Bible) and **Jan Hus** in Bohemia (early 15th century).
- **Rulers** of growing nation-states wanted control over Church lands and appointments; **merchants** resented Church taxes.

key_terms.definition_md: A scholar of the new learning who studied old writings with care.
A growing state under a ruler, with its own interests.

sections.heading: 3. Martin Luther's protest
sections.body_md:
- **Martin Luther** (1483 to 1546): a German monk and a professor at **Wittenberg**.
- **1517:** he made public the **Ninety-five Theses** against the **sale of indulgences**; **Johann Tetzel** was selling indulgences in Germany.
- **1521:** **Pope Leo X excommunicated** him; at the **Diet of Worms** he refused to take back his views.
- **Frederick of Saxony** protected him. He translated the **New Testament into German**, and later the whole Bible.

sections.heading: 4. Luther's main teachings
sections.body_md:
- **Salvation by faith** (justification by faith), not by buying indulgences.
- The **Bible** as the main authority.
- The **priesthood of all believers**: every believer may approach God directly.
- **Fewer sacraments:** baptism and communion.
- Services and the Bible in the **language of the people**.

sections.heading: 5. Effects of Luther's protest and other reformers
sections.body_md:
- **Lutheran churches** spread in **northern Germany** and **Scandinavia**.
- **Western Christianity was divided** into Catholic and Protestant churches.
- **Peace of Augsburg (1555):** each ruler in the German states chose the **Lutheran or Catholic** faith for his state.
- **Other reformers (one line each):** **Zwingli** in **Zurich**; **Calvin** in **Geneva**; in England **Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534)** made the king head of the Church of England.

sections.heading: 6. The Counter Reformation (Catholic Reformation)
sections.body_md:
- **Meaning:** measures by which the Catholic Church reformed itself and checked the spread of Protestantism.
- **Council of Trent (1545 to 1563):** reaffirmed Catholic doctrines; stopped the sale of indulgences for money; required better training of priests in seminaries; insisted on discipline among the clergy.
- **Society of Jesus (Jesuits):** founded by **Ignatius Loyola**, approved **1540**; worked in **education** and **missions** (Francis Xavier in Asia, see Chapter 14).
- **The Index** of prohibited books; Church courts against heresy (**the Inquisition**).
- **Results:** a reformed Catholic Church that remained strong in southern Europe.

key_terms.definition_md: The Catholic Church's own reform and its effort to check Protestantism.
Belief that the Church considered contrary to its teaching.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving a date without the word about, or forgetting that 1517 began the Reformation.
- Mixing up Erasmus (a scholar who criticised abuses) with Luther.
- Writing that each villager chose a faith at Augsburg; it was the ruler.
- Forgetting two sacraments (baptism and communion) or one of the five teachings.
- Confusing the Council of Trent with the Diet of Worms.
- Using sweeping words such as corrupt or evil; write that critics objected to certain practices.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or date.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a link, reasons or a result.

**Baptism and communion** only; services in the **language of the people**.
Lutheran churches in **northern Germany and Scandinavia**; Western Christianity **divided**.
Each **ruler** in the German states chose **Lutheran or Catholic** faith for his state.
Zwingli in **Zurich**; Calvin in **Geneva**.
Henry VIII; the **king became head of the Church of England**.
The Catholic Church's measures to **reform itself** and **check the spread of Protestantism**.
**1545 to 1563**: doctrines reaffirmed; indulgence sale for money stopped; **seminaries**; **discipline**.
Founded by **Ignatius Loyola**, approved **1540**; **education** and **missions**.
A Jesuit who worked in **Asia** (see Chapter 14).
A list of **books Catholics were told not to read**.
**Church courts** that dealt with **heresy**.
A **reformed** Catholic Church that remained **strong in southern Europe**.

questions.stem_md: A notice on the board of the imagined Weissburg University announces a talk titled The Reformation for visiting Class IX pupils. Which description should the speaker open with?

options.text_md: A movement that united all Christians in Europe under one church in the twelfth century
A sixteenth-century movement in Western Christianity that protested against certain practices of the Roman Catholic Church and led to Protestant churches
A sixteenth-century movement that began in Asia and reached Europe by sea
A revival of Greek and Roman art that began in Italian cities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A sixteenth-century movement in Western Christianity that protested against certain practices of the Roman Catholic Church and led to Protestant churches. The Reformation began in 1517 and led to Protestant churches. A union of all Christians describes the opposite, it did not begin in Asia, and the revival of art and learning is the Renaissance, a different movement.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined parish record of Kirchdorf, a baker named Anselm buys a printed certificate from a travelling seller, who says it will reduce the punishment for his sins. What is such a certificate called, and why did critics object to its sale?

options.text_md: A tithe; critics objected to paying one tenth of income to the Church
A sacrament; critics objected that it was performed in Latin
A thesis; critics objected that it was printed on paper
An indulgence; critics objected that forgiveness seemed to be put on sale for money

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** An indulgence; critics objected that forgiveness seemed to be put on sale for money. A certificate said to reduce punishment for sins is an indulgence, and its sale was one of the main practices critics objected to. A tithe is a Church tax, a sacrament is a religious rite, and a thesis is a statement put forward for debate.

questions.stem_md: A report from the imagined bishopric of Altmark says that a vacant Church office went to the candidate who offered the largest payment, not to the one best suited to the work. What is this practice called?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Simony. The sale of Church offices is simony. The tithe is a Church tax, excommunication is exclusion from the Church, and a Diet is an assembly of the German states.

questions.stem_md: Berta, an imagined farmer of Kirchdorf, notes in her account book that one tenth of her harvest goes to the Church every year. What was this payment called, and how did critics view it?

options.text_md: An indulgence; critics saw it as a certificate that reduced punishment for sins
Simony; critics saw it as the sale of Church offices
The tithe; critics saw it as part of the great wealth and heavy taxes of the Church
A thesis; critics saw it as a statement of belief

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The tithe; critics saw it as part of the great wealth and heavy taxes of the Church. One tenth of produce paid to the Church is the tithe, one of the taxes that critics mentioned along with the Church's wealth. The other terms describe different things.

questions.stem_md: Hilde, an imagined weaver of Kirchdorf, goes to church every week but says she cannot follow the words, because the service is in Latin. Which criticism of the time does her complaint illustrate?

options.text_md: The Church had stopped holding services
The Church courts had been closed
Services and the Bible were in Latin, which ordinary people did not understand
Priests had refused to accept any payment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Services and the Bible were in Latin, which ordinary people did not understand. Hilde cannot follow a Latin service, which is the language criticism. Nothing in her complaint says that services stopped, that courts closed or that priests refused payment.

questions.stem_md: A reading list in the imagined Weissburg library describes a Dutch scholar whose book The Praise of Folly, written about 1511, criticised abuses. Who is this scholar?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Erasmus. The Dutch humanist who wrote The Praise of Folly was Erasmus. Luther was German, Wycliffe was an earlier English reformer, and Loyola founded the Society of Jesus.

questions.stem_md: An imagined printer's order book at Rheinfeld shows 300 copies of a short pamphlet finished in three days, work that scribes copying by hand would have needed months to complete. Which cause of the Reformation does this best illustrate?

options.text_md: Rulers of growing nation-states wanted control over Church lands
The Council of Trent reformed the training of priests
Printing spread critical ideas and Bibles quickly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Printing spread critical ideas and Bibles quickly. Fast printing of many identical copies is the printing cause. The ruler and merchant causes are not mentioned in the order book, and the Council of Trent belongs to the Catholic response, after the Reformation began.

questions.stem_md: King Ottmar of the imagined kingdom of Altmark wants the lands owned by the Church in his kingdom to come under his control, and wants a say in who is appointed to Church posts. Which cause of the Reformation does this reflect?

options.text_md: Services in Latin were not understood by ordinary people
Rulers of growing nation-states wanted control over Church lands and appointments
Earlier reformers had translated the Bible into English

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rulers of growing nation-states wanted control over Church lands and appointments. A king seeking control over Church lands and appointments shows the political cause. Latin, printing and the English Bible are other causes, but the king's wishes are about power over the Church in his state.

questions.stem_md: The imagined guild of cloth merchants at Handelsbrunn complains that the taxes it must pay to the Church cut into its profits. Which cause of the Reformation does the complaint show?

options.text_md: Earlier reformers such as John Wycliffe

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Merchants resented Church taxes. A merchants' complaint about taxes paid to the Church is the cause that names merchants resenting Church taxes. Wycliffe, simony and Latin services are separate causes with no mention in the complaint.

questions.stem_md: A quiz slip at the imagined Weissburg History Club asks which pair correctly places two earlier reformers, John Wycliffe and Jan Hus, in their countries. Which pair is correct?

options.text_md: Wycliffe in Bohemia, Hus in England
Wycliffe in England, Hus in Bohemia
Wycliffe in Germany, Hus in Italy
Wycliffe in Spain, Hus in Portugal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Wycliffe in England, Hus in Bohemia. John Wycliffe of England (fourteenth century) and Jan Hus of Bohemia (early fifteenth century) came before Luther. The other pairs place them in the wrong countries.

questions.stem_md: A pupil of the imagined Weissburg Gymnasium lists causes of the Reformation and, by mistake, includes one item that was actually a later result. Which item is it?

options.text_md: The Council of Trent ended the sale of indulgences for money
Resentment of Church taxes among merchants

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Council of Trent ended the sale of indulgences for money. The Council of Trent met from 1545, long after 1517, so its decision is a result, part of the Catholic response. The other three came before or at the time the Reformation began.

questions.stem_md: A pupil's imagined essay on the Reformation opens with a sentence that condemns the whole Church and every priest. Which rewritten sentence is the most accurate and respectful for a history answer?

options.text_md: The reformers were wrong about everything, and their complaints had no basis
All the clergy were blameless, and the critics invented every complaint
The Church ceased to exist after 1517
Critics objected to certain Church practices, such as the sale of indulgences, and the Church later carried out reforms of its own

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Critics objected to certain Church practices, such as the sale of indulgences, and the Church later carried out reforms of its own. A balanced answer names the practices critics objected to and notes the Church's own reforms. The other versions condemn one side, deny all complaints, or are untrue because the Church continued after 1517.

questions.stem_md: A museum card in the imagined town of Weissburg describes a German monk and professor at Wittenberg who made public his Ninety-five Theses in 1517. Who is described?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Martin Luther. Martin Luther (1483 to 1546) was the German monk and professor at Wittenberg. Erasmus was a Dutch scholar, Loyola founded the Jesuits, and Leo X was the Pope of the time.

questions.stem_md: An imagined chronicle of Weissburg records that Johann Tetzel was selling indulgences nearby, and that a professor at Wittenberg answered by making public his Ninety-five Theses. What did the Theses protest against?

options.text_md: The building of printing presses in Germany
The teaching of Greek at universities
The founding of the Society of Jesus

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The sale of indulgences. Luther's Theses were directed against the sale of indulgences. Printing presses and Greek teaching were not their target, and the Society of Jesus was founded later, in the 1540s.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined clerk's diary dated 1521, a monk is summoned before an assembly of German princes and officials in a city on the Rhine and is asked to take back his writings. He refuses. Which assembly is this, and who was the monk?

options.text_md: The Council of Trent; Ignatius Loyola
The Diet of Worms; Martin Luther
The Peace of Augsburg; John Calvin

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Diet of Worms; Martin Luther. An assembly in 1521 where Luther refused to take back his views was the Diet of Worms. The Council of Trent began in 1545, Augsburg dates from 1555, and Erasmus was not summoned to Worms.

questions.stem_md: An imagined note by a ballad-sheet seller records that a ruler of Saxony sheltered a monk after 1521, and that during this time the monk translated the New Testament into German. Who was the ruler, and why did the translation matter?

options.text_md: Frederick of Saxony; ordinary Germans could read the New Testament in their own language
Pope Leo X; the translation was ordered for use in Latin services
Frederick of Saxony; the translation ended every church service in Latin across Europe at once
Henry VIII; the translation made the king head of the Church

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Frederick of Saxony; ordinary Germans could read the New Testament in their own language. Frederick of Saxony protected Luther, and the German New Testament let ordinary readers meet the text directly. Leo X excommunicated Luther, Latin services did not end overnight, and Henry VIII belongs to England.

questions.stem_md: Hanna, an imagined weaver of Nordburg, is told that her sins can be forgiven only after she buys a certificate. A preacher who follows Luther tells her instead that she is saved by faith. Which teaching of Luther does the preacher state?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Salvation by faith (justification by faith). Luther taught salvation by faith rather than by buying indulgences. Priesthood of all believers is a different teaching, Luther wanted services in the language of the people, and he kept only two sacraments.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined meeting in Nordburg's market hall, a speaker says that every believer may read the Bible and approach God directly, without a priest as a necessary go-between. Which teaching of Luther is this?

options.text_md: Church courts as the final authority
The Pope's command over every ruler

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The priesthood of all believers. Every believer able to approach God directly is the priesthood of all believers. Buying indulgences, final authority of Church courts and the Pope's command over rulers are not Luther's teachings.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined diary of a clerk in 1555, Prince Wilhelm of Nordburg announces that his state will follow the Lutheran faith, while the prince of the neighbouring state keeps the Catholic faith. Which arrangement allowed this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Peace of Augsburg. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each ruler choose Lutheran or Catholic faith for his state. The Council of Trent was a Catholic council, the Act of Supremacy concerned England, and Worms was in 1521.

questions.stem_md: A quiz card in the imagined Weissburg Reformation gallery pairs reformers with cities. Which pairing is correct?

options.text_md: Zwingli with Geneva and Calvin with Zurich
Luther with Geneva and Calvin with Wittenberg
Zwingli with Zurich and Calvin with Geneva
Zwingli with Wittenberg and Luther with Zurich

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Zwingli with Zurich and Calvin with Geneva. Zwingli worked in Zurich, Calvin in Geneva, and Luther in Wittenberg. The other pairings mix these cities up.

questions.stem_md: The imagined bishop of Sankt Elmar reads the decisions of the Council of Trent and opens a seminary in his town to train young priests properly. Which aim of the Council does his act serve?

options.text_md: The sale of indulgences for money
The translation of the Bible into German
Better training of priests in seminaries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Better training of priests in seminaries. Seminaries for training priests were a decision of the Council of Trent. The Council stopped the sale of indulgences for money, the German Bible was Luther's work, and the Act of Supremacy concerned England.

questions.stem_md: A school in the imagined town of Sankt Elmar is run by members of the Society of Jesus. In which two fields did the Jesuits mainly work?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Education and missions. The Jesuits, founded by Ignatius Loyola and approved in 1540, worked mainly in education and missions. The other fields were not their main work.

questions.stem_md: A librarian in the imagined city of Neustadt keeps a list, issued by the Catholic Church, of books that Catholics were told not to read. What was this list called?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Index of prohibited books. The Church's list of books was the Index of prohibited books. The Theses were Luther's statements, the Act of Supremacy concerned England, and Augsburg was a settlement among German states.

questions.stem_md: An imagined history teacher in Neustadt tells the class that the Inquisition formed part of the Catholic Church's response to Protestantism. Which description of the Inquisition is correct and neutral?

options.text_md: A teaching order founded by Ignatius Loyola
Church courts that dealt with questions of heresy, that is, belief the Church considered contrary to its teaching
A council that met at Trent from 1545 to 1563
A list of books that Catholics were told not to read

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Church courts that dealt with questions of heresy, that is, belief the Church considered contrary to its teaching. The Inquisition means the Church courts that dealt with heresy. A teaching order describes the Jesuits, the council was Trent, and the list was the Index.

questions.stem_md: An imagined atlas lesson compares Europe in about 1600. Northern Germany and Scandinavia have Lutheran churches, while Spain, Italy and Portugal remain mainly Catholic. Which result of the Counter Reformation does the southern part of the map show?

options.text_md: The Catholic Church was reformed and remained strong in southern Europe
The Catholic Church disappeared from Europe
The Pope became head of the Church of England

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Catholic Church was reformed and remained strong in southern Europe. The map shows a reformed Catholic Church that stayed strong in the south. It did not disappear, Europe did not all become Lutheran, and the Church of England has the king as head after 1534.

questions.stem_md: On the imagined timeline poster in the Weissburg gallery, the Council of Trent is shown as a shaded bar. Which years does the bar cover?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1545 to 1563. The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563. The other spans do not match the Council: 1517 to 1521 covers Luther's protest and the Diet of Worms.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Printed pamphlets and Bibles helped critical ideas to spread widely and quickly in sixteenth-century Europe.

**Reason (R):** A printing press could produce many identical copies much faster than scribes copying by hand.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Fast, cheap copying is exactly why printed material travelled so far, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Critics argued that services and the Bible in Latin kept many ordinary people from understanding them.

**Reason (R):** Latin was the everyday spoken language of most ordinary people across Western Europe.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: people spoke their own regional languages, which is why Latin was hard for them to follow.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** By the Peace of Augsburg (1555), every villager in the German states was free to choose the Lutheran or the Catholic faith for himself.

**Reason (R):** The Peace of Augsburg allowed each ruler in the German states to choose the Lutheran or the Catholic faith for his state.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the choice was made by the ruler, not by each villager. R states the settlement correctly.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Council of Trent required better training of priests in seminaries.

**Reason (R):** The Catholic Church wished to improve the learning and discipline of its clergy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. The wish to improve learning and discipline among the clergy is the reason behind the seminaries, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Jesuits worked in education and missions.

**Reason (R):** The Society of Jesus was approved in 1540, before the Council of Trent began.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but the date of approval does not explain what kind of work the Jesuits did, so R is not the explanation of A.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A pupil at the imagined Weissburg school says that the Reformation ended with the formation of one single Protestant church which all reformers joined.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Several Protestant churches formed, for example the Lutheran churches, the churches of Zwingli and Calvin, and the Church of England.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An imagined chronicler of Weissburg writes that Pope Leo X excommunicated Martin Luther in 1521.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther in 1521, the year of the Diet of Worms.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An imagined lecturer at Neustadt says that the Counter Reformation was the Catholic Church's effort to reform itself and to check the spread of Protestantism.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The Counter Reformation, also called the Catholic Reformation, means exactly these measures of the Catholic Church.

questions.stem_md: Martin Luther was a German monk and a professor at the university of ___.
questions.solution_md: Luther taught at the university of Wittenberg.

questions.stem_md: The Council of Trent began its meetings in ___ and ended them in ___.
questions.solution_md: The Council of Trent met from 1545 and ended in 1563.

questions.stem_md: The Society of Jesus, approved in ___, was founded by Ignatius ___.
questions.solution_md: Ignatius Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, which was approved in 1540.

questions.stem_md: Each imagined scene below shows one cause of the Reformation. Match each scene with the cause it illustrates.

options.text_md: A parish in Kirchdorf is asked to hand over a tenth of its harvest
A Church post in Altmark goes to the highest bidder
A printer in Rheinfeld quickly prints a Bible for local readers
King Ottmar wants a say in Church appointments

match_right.text_md: Rulers wanting control of Church lands and appointments
Great wealth and taxes of the Church

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). A tenth of the harvest is the tithe, a post sold for payment is simony, quick printing is the printing cause, and the king's wish is the political cause.

questions.stem_md: A display in the imagined Weissburg gallery shows four names. Match each name with the right description.

match_right.text_md: German reformer whose followers formed Lutheran churches
A reformer who worked in Zurich
King whose Act of Supremacy (1534) made him head of the Church of England
A reformer who worked in Geneva

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Zwingli is linked with Zurich, Calvin with Geneva, Henry VIII with the Act of Supremacy of 1534, and Luther with the Lutheran churches.

questions.stem_md: A pupil at the imagined Neustadt school prepares four cards on the Counter Reformation. Match each card with its description.

match_right.text_md: Church courts that dealt with heresy
A list of books Catholics were told not to read
Reaffirmed Catholic doctrines and required seminaries for priests

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The Council of Trent reaffirmed doctrines and required seminaries, the Jesuits taught and went on missions, the Index was the book list, and the Inquisition means Church courts for heresy.

questions.stem_md: Four cards are pinned on the imagined timeline wall of the Weissburg gallery. Arrange them in the order in which the events happened.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). The Theses came first in 1517, then the Diet of Worms in 1521, the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 and the end of the Council of Trent in 1563.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: A pupil at the imagined Neustadt school arranges four events of the Catholic Church's response in time order, adding the Augsburg settlement for context. Arrange them.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (b) → (d). The Jesuits were approved in 1540, the Council opened in 1545, the Peace of Augsburg followed in 1555, and the Council closed in 1563.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: A visitor to the imagined Weissburg gallery asks what the Reformation was and when it began. Answer in two points.
questions.solution_md: Movement, protest, Protestant churches; 1517.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Reformation** was a **sixteenth-century movement** in Western Christianity that protested against certain practices of the Roman Catholic Church and led to the formation of **Protestant churches**. It began in **1517**.

marking_scheme.step: A sixteenth-century movement that protested against certain Church practices and led to Protestant churches

questions.stem_md: Who was Erasmus, and how did his writing contribute to the Reformation? Name one of his works.
questions.solution_md: Dutch scholar; his writings criticised abuses.

answer.model_answer_md: **Erasmus** was a **Dutch humanist scholar**. His writings, such as **The Praise of Folly** (about 1511), criticised abuses and encouraged readers to question, which helped the new learning.

marking_scheme.step: Dutch humanist scholar whose writings criticised abuses

questions.stem_md: King Ottmar of the imagined kingdom of Altmark and the cloth merchants of Handelsbrunn both favour reform for reasons that are not only about belief. State one such reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Control over lands for the king; taxes for merchants.

answer.model_answer_md: **King Ottmar:** as a ruler of a growing nation-state he wanted **control over Church lands and appointments**. **Merchants:** they **resented the taxes** they paid to the Church, which reduced their profits.

marking_scheme.step: Ruler: control over Church lands and appointments

questions.stem_md: A pupil preparing a talk on the imagined parish of Kirchdorf must explain two terms that critics used. Explain the tithe and simony.
questions.solution_md: Tithe: a Church tax; simony: sale of offices.

answer.model_answer_md: The **tithe** was a Church tax of about one tenth of produce or income, which critics linked with the Church's great wealth. **Simony** was the **sale of Church offices**, which critics said put posts in the hands of those who paid.

marking_scheme.step: Tithe: a Church tax of about one tenth
Simony: the sale of Church offices

questions.stem_md: What action did Pope Leo X take against Martin Luther in 1521, and how did Luther respond at the Diet of Worms?
questions.solution_md: Excommunicated; refused to take back his views.

answer.model_answer_md: **Pope Leo X** **excommunicated** Luther in **1521**. When he appeared before the **Diet of Worms**, an assembly of German princes and officials, Luther **refused to take back his views**.

marking_scheme.step: Excommunicated by Pope Leo X in 1521
Refused to take back his views at the Diet of Worms

questions.stem_md: In an imagined letter from Weissburg, a student asks why a Wittenberg professor made public Ninety-five Theses in 1517. Answer in two points, naming the seller of indulgences involved.
questions.solution_md: Protest against indulgences; Tetzel.

answer.model_answer_md: Luther made public the **Ninety-five Theses** in **1517** to protest against the **sale of indulgences**. **Johann Tetzel** was selling them in Germany at the time.

marking_scheme.step: Protest against the sale of indulgences in 1517
Johann Tetzel named as the seller

questions.stem_md: State what the Peace of Augsburg (1555) decided about the faith of the German states.
questions.solution_md: Each ruler chose the faith of his state.

answer.model_answer_md: Under the **Peace of Augsburg**, **each ruler** in the German states could **choose** either the **Lutheran or the Catholic faith** for his state, so Lutheranism was recognised beside Catholicism.

marking_scheme.step: Each ruler chose Lutheran or Catholic faith for his state

questions.stem_md: Who founded the Society of Jesus, and what two kinds of work did its members do?
questions.solution_md: Ignatius Loyola; education and missions.

answer.model_answer_md: The Society of Jesus was founded by **Ignatius Loyola** and approved in **1540**. Its members, the Jesuits, worked in **education** and in **missions**; Francis Xavier, for example, went to Asia.

questions.stem_md: The imagined bishop of Sankt Elmar opens a seminary and reminds his priests to follow rules of discipline. State two decisions of the Council of Trent that he is putting into effect.
questions.solution_md: Seminaries and discipline.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Council of Trent** called for **seminaries to train priests better** and for **discipline among the clergy**. It also stopped the sale of indulgences for money and reaffirmed Catholic doctrines.

marking_scheme.step: Better training of priests in seminaries

questions.stem_md: What was the Index of prohibited books, and which body issued it?
questions.solution_md: Church list of banned books.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Index** was the Church's **list of books** that Catholics were told to avoid. The **Catholic Church** issued it as a Counter Reformation measure, to check the spread of Protestant ideas.

marking_scheme.step: A list of books Catholics were told not to read
Issued by the Catholic Church as a Counter Reformation measure

questions.stem_md: At an imagined debate in the Weissburg town hall, speakers list practices of the Church that people objected to before 1517. State any three.
questions.solution_md: Any three practices.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **sale of indulgences**, certificates said to reduce punishment for sins.
2. The **sale of Church offices** (simony).

marking_scheme.step: First practice with a clear statement
Second practice with a clear statement
Third practice with a clear statement

questions.stem_md: A teacher at the imagined Handelsbrunn school says that the new learning prepared the ground for the Reformation. Explain this with reference to the Renaissance, Erasmus and printing.
questions.solution_md: Enquiry; Erasmus; printing.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Renaissance spirit of enquiry** encouraged people to question authority.
2. **Humanist scholars** such as **Erasmus** wrote works, like The Praise of Folly, that criticised abuses.
3. **Printing** spread critical ideas and Bibles quickly to many readers.

questions.stem_md: A guide in the imagined Nordburg church hall is asked about the main teachings of Martin Luther. State any three.
questions.solution_md: Any three teachings.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Salvation by faith**, also called justification by faith, in place of buying indulgences.
2. The **Bible** as the chief authority.
3. The **priesthood of all believers**; he also kept fewer **sacraments** (baptism and communion) and wanted services in the **language of the people**.

marking_scheme.step: The Bible as the main authority
One more teaching: priesthood of all believers, two sacraments or services in local language

questions.stem_md: An imagined map-maker of Neustadt shades the regions that followed Luther. Describe three effects of Luther's protest on Europe.
questions.solution_md: Spread; division; Augsburg and other reformers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. New **Lutheran churches** grew up across **northern Germany** and **Scandinavia**.
2. Christianity in the West **split** into Catholic and Protestant churches.
3. The **Peace of Augsburg** (1555) let each German ruler choose Lutheran or Catholic faith, and **other reformers** such as Zwingli and Calvin followed.

Peace of Augsburg or other reformers

questions.stem_md: A student of the imagined Weissburg club writes one line each on Zwingli, Calvin and Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy. Write what she should say.
questions.solution_md: Zurich; Geneva; Church of England.

questions.stem_md:
In the imagined university town of Weissburg, a lecture is advertised on why dissatisfaction with the Church grew before 1517.

(i) State three practices of the Church that critics objected to. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the Renaissance spirit of enquiry, Erasmus and printing helped the Reformation. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how rulers, merchants and earlier reformers contributed. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Practices; new learning; rulers, merchants and earlier reformers.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Critics objected to the **sale of indulgences**, the **sale of Church offices** (simony) and the **great wealth and taxes** of the Church, such as the tithe. Some also pointed to the worldly lives of some clergy and to services in Latin.

(ii) The **Renaissance** encouraged people to question authority. **Erasmus**, a Dutch scholar, criticised abuses in works such as **The Praise of Folly**. **Printing** spread critical ideas and Bibles quickly.

(iii) **Rulers** of growing nation-states wanted **control over Church lands and appointments**, and **merchants** resented Church taxes. Earlier reformers, **John Wycliffe** in England and **Jan Hus** in Bohemia, had shown that dissatisfaction was not new.

questions.stem_md:
At an imagined market meeting in Handelsbrunn, three people speak: Jakob, a printer who is busy with Bible orders, Duke Berthold, who wants to appoint the heads of Church lands in his duchy, and Greta, a cloth merchant who objects to Church taxes.

(i) Name the cause of the Reformation that each speaker best represents. **[3]**
(ii) Explain why Wycliffe and Hus show that dissatisfaction with Church practices was not new. **[3]**
(iii) A listener claims that the Reformation was caused only by the sale of indulgences. Evaluate this view. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Causes matched; earlier reformers; evaluation of a single cause.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Jakob** represents the spread of ideas through **printing**. **Duke Berthold** represents rulers of growing states who wanted **control over Church lands and appointments**. **Greta** represents **merchants who resented Church taxes**.

(ii) **John Wycliffe** in England in the fourteenth century had an English translation of the Bible made, and **Jan Hus** in Bohemia in the early fifteenth century also criticised practices. This was long before 1517, so unease had been growing.

(iii) The view is **only partly true**. The sale of indulgences led Luther to speak out in 1517, but the Reformation also had other causes: the **new learning**, **printing**, the wishes of **rulers** and **merchants**, and earlier reformers. Many causes worked together.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Hus with detail and earlier dates

questions.stem_md:
A display at the imagined Weissburg museum is titled A Monk Who Spoke Out.

(i) Who was Martin Luther, and what did his Ninety-five Theses protest against? **[3]**
(ii) Describe what happened to Luther in 1521. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how Frederick of Saxony and the translation of the Bible helped Luther's cause. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Luther and his protest; 1521; protection and translation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Martin Luther** (1483 to 1546) was a **German monk and professor at Wittenberg**. In **1517** he made public the **Ninety-five Theses** against the **sale of indulgences**, which **Johann Tetzel** was selling in Germany.

(ii) In **1521** **Pope Leo X excommunicated** him. He then appeared before the **Diet of Worms**, where he **refused to take back his views**.

(iii) **Frederick of Saxony** protected Luther, so he could work in safety. Luther translated the **New Testament into German**, and later the whole Bible, so ordinary people could read it in their own language. With **printing**, the translation spread his ideas widely.

marking_scheme.step: (i) German monk and professor at Wittenberg
(ii) Refused to take back his views at the Diet of Worms
(iii) German translation read by ordinary people

questions.stem_md:
A teacher at the imagined Nordburg school draws a chart of the main teachings of Martin Luther.

(i) State three of his teachings. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the teaching of the priesthood of all believers and the teaching on sacraments. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how these teachings differed from the practices that critics had objected to. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Three teachings; priesthood and sacraments; contrast with practices.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Luther taught **salvation by faith** (justification by faith), the **Bible as the main authority**, and services in the **language of the people**.

(ii) The **priesthood of all believers** means every believer may approach God directly and read the Bible without a priest as a necessary go-between. Luther kept **fewer sacraments**: **baptism and communion**.

(iii) Critics had objected to the **sale of indulgences**, and Luther taught that salvation comes by **faith** and cannot be bought. Critics had noted services in **Latin** that people could not follow, and Luther wanted worship and the Bible in the **language of the people**. The Bible, not Church offices, became the main authority.

questions.stem_md:
A teacher in the imagined town of Nordburg asks pupils to describe the results of Luther's protest.

(i) Describe how Lutheran churches spread and how Western Christianity was affected. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the Peace of Augsburg (1555). **[3]**
(iii) Write one line each on Zwingli, Calvin and the Act of Supremacy (1534), and say what they show about the spread of reform. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Spread and division; Augsburg; other reformers and what they show.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Lutheran churches** took root in **northern Germany** and **Scandinavia**. The unity of **Western Christianity was broken**, with Catholic and Protestant churches side by side.

(ii) By the **Peace of Augsburg** (1555) **each ruler** in the German states chose the **Lutheran or Catholic faith** for his state, which recognised Lutheranism beside Catholicism.

(iii) **Zwingli** led reform in **Zurich** and **Calvin** in **Geneva**. In England, **Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy** (1534) made the **king head of the Church of England**. These show that reform did not stay in one place: other reformers followed, and in different lands rulers and cities shaped what the new churches looked like.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Spread in northern Germany and Scandinavia
(ii) Each ruler chose the faith of his state
(iii) Reform did not stay in one place

questions.stem_md:
The history club of the imagined town of Sankt Elmar prepares a poster on how the Catholic Church responded to the Reformation.

(i) What is meant by the Counter Reformation? Name two decisions of the Council of Trent. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the work of the Society of Jesus. **[3]**
(iii) Mention the Index and the Inquisition, and state two results of the Counter Reformation. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and Trent; Jesuits; Index, Inquisition, results.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Counter Reformation**, or Catholic Reformation, means the **measures by which the Catholic Church reformed itself and checked the spread of Protestantism**. The **Council of Trent** (1545 to 1563) **reaffirmed Catholic doctrines** and **required seminaries** to train priests.

(ii) The **Society of Jesus**, founded by **Ignatius Loyola** and approved in **1540**, worked in **education** and **missions**. **Francis Xavier**, for example, worked in Asia.

(iii) The Church issued the **Index of prohibited books**, and Church courts against heresy, the **Inquisition**, were used. The results were that the Catholic Church was **reformed** and remained **strong in southern Europe**.

questions.stem_md:
Two groups at the imagined Weissburg school compare the Protestant Reformation with the Catholic response, and they agree to describe both with equal respect.

(i) State three teachings or aims of the Lutheran Reformation. **[3]**
(ii) State three measures of the Counter Reformation. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how these two movements changed the religious map of Europe. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Teachings; measures; the changed map.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Salvation by faith**, the **Bible as the main authority** and the **priesthood of all believers** were central Lutheran teachings; they also taught fewer sacraments and services in the language of the people.

(ii) The **Council of Trent** reaffirmed doctrines and required seminaries, the **Society of Jesus** worked in education and missions, and the **Index** listed prohibited books.

(iii) The Reformation **divided Western Christianity**, and Lutheran churches spread in **northern Germany and Scandinavia**. The Counter Reformation **reformed the Catholic Church**, which remained **strong in southern Europe**. By the **Peace of Augsburg** (1555), each German ruler chose Lutheran or Catholic faith for his state, so both traditions continued.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Catholic Church reformed and strong in the south
